title: Two Evenings at the Community Hub
text:
The Eastbridge Community Hub closes at 6:00 p.m. on weekdays, even though several of its most-used services are aimed at people who are at work or in class during the day. I believe the city should keep the hub open until 8:00 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays for a six-month trial. The goal is not to turn the building into a late-night center. It is to make existing services reachable at the times when many residents can actually use them.

The strongest reason is access. Last spring, the hub tracked when visitors arrived for its job-search computers, language tutoring, and document-help desk. Between 4:30 and 6:00 p.m., those services were used at nearly twice the rate seen between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. Staff also recorded 86 people who arrived during the final half hour and had to leave before finishing a form, tutoring session, or online application. Those numbers do not prove that every evening would be busy, but they show that demand rises as the current closing time approaches.

A limited evening schedule could also use staff time more efficiently than opening later every night. The library branch next door already keeps two security officers on the block until 8:30 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Under a preliminary estimate from the hub manager, shifting two staff members to later hours on those days would cost far less than adding a separate evening shift five nights a week. The city could therefore test extended access without committing to the most expensive version of the idea.

Some residents have raised a fair concern: longer hours could increase costs even if attendance remains low. That is why the proposal should include a clear review point. For six months, the hub should record evening visits, the services used, staffing costs, and any security incidents. If the extended hours attract few residents or create costs that the benefits do not justify, the city should end or revise the trial rather than making it permanent.

The trial should also stay focused on services that residents already use. It would be a mistake to add concerts, new classes, or a cafe simply to make the evening hours look successful. Those additions would make it difficult to tell whether later access itself helped. Keeping the program narrow would let the city answer a simpler question: does opening two hours later on two carefully chosen weekdays help more people use the services the hub already provides?

Eastbridge does not need to guess whether a full expansion will work. It can test a smaller claim first. By extending the hub's hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays, measuring actual use and cost, and reviewing the results after six months, the city can improve access while limiting financial risk. If the evidence is strong, the city can consider expanding the schedule. If it is weak, officials can stop without having built an expensive permanent program.
